title: The Lantern of Numeria — a 17-chapter story spine
status: pilot implementation in progress — lesson 1-1 applied
premise: In present-day Jeddah, two fictional Grade 4 archivists, Omar and Zayd, find a brass lantern holding a water-damaged civic design journal. Their class restores seventeen linked folios and uses each recovered idea to design Numeria: an explicitly fictional exhibition city built on amanah, evidence and beneficial knowledge.
drivingQuestion: How can mathematics help us design a city that deserves people’s trust?

influences.oneThousandAndOneNights: Borrow the craft, not the plots: a frame narrator, nested accounts, recurring objects, delayed answers, callbacks and a clean cliffhanger at the end of each lesson.
influences.oneThousandInventions: Use source-checked episodes from the history of science and engineering as STEM provocations. Present knowledge as cumulative and cross-cultural; avoid simplistic “X invented Y” claims.
influences.seerah: Use a separate, source-approved Amanah Window for chronology, character and values. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions are never fictional characters, avatars, game pieces or suppliers of invented data.

characters.rolePolicy: Both boys reason, build, question, revise and sometimes make incomplete claims. Their lead role alternates so Omar is not always correct and Zayd is not only the hands-on character.
characters.visualPolicy: Original age-appropriate flat vector boys in modest contemporary clothing. They never resemble or represent the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, his companions or any historical person.

screenDesign.principle: The lesson earns its number of screens from the mathematics, student actions and available class time. Keep a stable learning arc, never a fixed slide count. A screen exists only when it introduces one distinct cognitive or collaborative act.
screenDesign.typicalSpan: Most lessons will use 7–16 screens, but this is an observed planning span—not a global minimum or maximum.

phases.label: Recall or cold open
phases.move: Use a brief callback when prior evidence is needed. The first lesson in a chapter uses a cold open instead; compact continuation lessons may merge recall into the need.

phases.label: Create the need
phases.move: Present the unresolved object, decision or contradiction. Students notice, predict or estimate before being taught a procedure.

phases.label: Struggle and investigate
phases.move: Give enough screens for genuinely different models, tests, constraints or revisions. Do not manufacture complications merely to lengthen the deck.

phases.label: Connect student voices
phases.move: Compare selected student strategies. A third screen is justified only when it adds a meaningfully different representation or misconception.

phases.label: Name and consolidate
phases.move: Draw the core idea on the board and name the transferable principle. A STEM history or approved Amanah Window may be embedded or follow here.

phases.label: Decision and evidence
phases.move: Students independently use the mathematics, then defend the story decision or add evidence to the PBL artifact.

phases.label: Consequence and handoff
phases.move: Show what the mathematics changed and reveal the exact object or unanswered need that opens the next lesson.

lessonShapes.label: Compact practice
lessonShapes.useWhen: Prior concepts are secure and the lesson adds fluency, estimation or one efficient strategy. Recall and need are usually combined.

lessonShapes.label: Strategy workshop
lessonShapes.useWhen: Students compare, select or practise methods without needing a long new conceptual model.

lessonShapes.label: Concept discovery
lessonShapes.useWhen: A new relationship or classification must be noticed, represented and named.

lessonShapes.label: Model investigation
lessonShapes.useWhen: Students need multiple concrete, visual and symbolic representations or must build/test a model.

lessonShapes.label: Application / PBL lab
lessonShapes.useWhen: Measurement, data, money, time or design work needs setup, collection, testing and revision.

lessonShapes.label: Reasoning studio
lessonShapes.useWhen: The standard foregrounds argument, critique, modelling, perseverance, precision or a unit-level decision.

authorDecisionRules: Start from minutes and student actions, not a target number of slides.
Add a screen only for a new question, representation, student action, evidence set, misconception, decision or accessibility scaffold.
Merge recall with the hook when the previous artifact itself creates today’s need.
Keep several screens for one investigation when students need time; screen count does not equal pacing speed.
Place at most one substantial STEM history or Amanah Window in a lesson. It may be a panel rather than a separate slide.
Cut any screen that only repeats exposition, decorates the story or reveals an answer students should construct.
Teacher navigation, progress indicators, verification and browser sweeps must read LESSON.metas.length dynamically.

guardrails: Narrative overhead is capped at about 90 seconds at the opening and 45 seconds at the close; mathematical work remains the mechanic.
Numeria, Omar, Zayd, the lantern and all civic missions are labelled fictional. Historical STEM and Seerah cards use a visibly different “documented account” treatment.
No visual depiction of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ or the named companions; use calligraphy-free object, place, manuscript or material-culture imagery approved by the school.
No invented dialogue, quantities, motives or transactions are attributed to sacred figures. No sacred event becomes a battle, optimization, reward or role-play game.
Every Seerah card carries a source field, reviewer, review date and approval status before it can appear to students.
Every STEM claim distinguishes invention, development, description, transmission and later reconstruction. A source check is required before publication.
Projects are assessed with mathematics, reasoning, design process and reflection—not costumes, story recall or points for clicking.
One project artifact per unit is enough. Lessons add evidence to it; they do not launch 114 separate craft projects.

units.chapter: The census in the brass lantern
units.act: Act I · Number, provision and systems
units.question: Can the class recover a damaged city census without changing what any digit means?
units.artifact: A restored census folio and place-value key
units.stem: How positional numerals and written calculation supported astronomy, trade and administration across the medieval Islamic world.
units.seerah: Chronology window: Makkah before revelation. Al-Amin and the meaning of trust. Use only a source-approved account; no portrait, role-play or invented transaction.
units.pbl: Teams prepare a one-page population and services brief for the fictional city of Numeria.
units.bridge: The recovered population is much larger than expected. The council cannot plan services until the damaged budget ledger is audited.

lessons.studentMission: Read, write and represent the population so the archivist can restore the first line.

units.curriculumTitle: Fluently Add and Subtract Multi-Digit Whole Numbers
units.chapter: The souq ledger with the missing total
units.act: Act I · Number, provision and systems
units.question: Can the class make a public budget trustworthy when part of the ledger is damaged?
units.stem: Bookkeeping, paper, written algorithms and the civic need for reliable accounts. Historical claims are framed as documented practices, not single-person “inventions.”
units.seerah: Chronology window: the first revelation and the command to read. Connect knowledge with responsibility; keep the sacred account separate from the fictional budget.
units.pbl: Create and peer-audit a budget for school reading corners using whole-number operations.
units.bridge: The audit is correct, but one order card lists each item in repeated batches. The workshop needs multiplication, not repeated addition.
